question: The king of the Greek gods hurled thunderbolts from his throne on Mount Olympus and ruled the sky. He overthrew his own father, Cronos, to take power. Who was he?
context: Zeus was the youngest son of Cronos and Rhea. His thunderbolts were forged by the Cyclopes deep in the earth. His sacred bird was the eagle and his sacred tree the oak. He won his kingdom by drawing lots with his brothers Poseidon and Hades after their war against the Titans.

question: The queen of the gods on Mount Olympus drove a chariot pulled by peacocks. She was Zeus's wife and his fiercest jealous rival. Who was she?
context: Hera was goddess of marriage and queen of the heavens. The peacock's hundred eyes came from her servant Argus, slain by Hermes — she set the eyes into her bird's tail to honor him. She pursued Zeus's many lovers without mercy, especially Io and Hercules.

question: The god of the sea, of horses, and of earthquakes shook the ground with the strike of a three-pronged spear. Sailors prayed to him before every voyage. What was his three-pronged spear called?
context: Poseidon was Zeus's brother. He created the first horse and gave it as a gift to humans. With his trident he could split rocks open or call up storms. The city of Athens almost named itself after him before Athena's olive tree won out.

question: The grim god who ruled the Greek land of the dead wore a magical helmet that made him invisible. The dog Cerberus guarded his gate. Who was he?
context: Hades was Zeus's brother. His helm of invisibility was forged for him by the Cyclopes during the war with the Titans. He kidnapped Persephone to be his queen. The Greeks feared even speaking his name and called him 'the rich one' (Plouton) instead.

question: When Zeus had a terrible headache, Hephaestus split his skull with an axe. Out leaped a fully-armed warrior goddess in a bronze helmet. Who came out of Zeus's head?
context: Athena was goddess of wisdom, weaving, and strategic war. Her sacred bird was the owl. She gave Athens the olive tree to win the city's patronage from Poseidon. She helped Perseus kill Medusa and guided Odysseus home.

question: The Olympian god of music, poetry, and the sun played a golden lyre and gave prophecies through his priestess at Delphi. His twin sister was Artemis. Who was he?
context: Apollo's first lyre was made by the baby Hermes from a tortoise shell. At Delphi, his oracle was the Pythia, a priestess who breathed vapors rising from a crack in the earth. He killed the giant serpent Python there as a young god.

question: The Greek goddess of the moon and the hunt ran with a pack of hounds and never missed a shot from her silver bow. Her twin brother was Apollo. Who was she?
context: Artemis was the protector of young girls and wild animals. She turned the hunter Actaeon into a stag for spying on her bathing, and his own hounds tore him apart. Her temple at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

question: The Olympian god of war and bloodshed loved battle for its own sake and rode a chariot pulled by four fire-breathing horses. He carried a long spear into combat. Who was he?
context: Ares was the son of Zeus and Hera. The other gods disliked him — even his father called him the most hated of all the Olympians. His sons Phobos (fear) and Deimos (terror) drove his chariot. He was Aphrodite's secret lover.

question: The Olympian messenger god wore winged sandals on his feet and a winged cap on his head. He carried a herald's staff twined with two serpents. What was the staff's name?
context: Hermes was the patron of travelers, traders, and thieves, and guide of the dead down to Hades. On his first day alive, the baby Hermes invented the lyre from a tortoise shell and stole Apollo's cattle by driving them backwards to hide their tracks.

question: The Olympian god of wine and theater rode in a chariot pulled by spotted panthers. He carried a fennel staff topped with a pine cone. Who was he?
context: Dionysus was born twice — once from his mortal mother Semele, then sewn into Zeus's thigh after her death to finish growing. His staff was called the thyrsus. His followers, the maenads, tore animals apart in his frenzied rites.

question: The Olympian goddess of love and beauty was not born of any mother. She rose fully grown from white sea foam off the island of Cyprus. Who was she?
context: Her name means 'foam-born' (from the Greek aphros). She rode the foam to shore on a scallop shell. She was married to the lame smith Hephaestus but loved the war god Ares — Hephaestus once caught them with a net of invisible bronze chains.

question: The Olympian smith god limped from a fall off Mount Olympus. He worked his forge deep under a volcano in Sicily called Mount Etna. Who was he?
context: Hera threw him off Olympus for being ugly, breaking his leg. He forged Zeus's thunderbolts, Poseidon's trident, Achilles's armor, and the chains that bound Prometheus. His helpers were the one-eyed Cyclopes — Brontes, Steropes, and Arges.

question: The Greek goddess of grain and the harvest had a daughter named Persephone taken to the underworld. The mother's grief froze the earth and brought the first winter. Who was she?
context: Demeter searched the whole earth for her daughter, refusing to let crops grow until Persephone was returned. Zeus made Hades release her, but Persephone had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld — so she must return there each winter.

question: The eldest sister of Zeus tended the sacred fire that burned in every Greek home and every city's main hall. She had no temples — every hearth was her shrine. Who was she?
context: Hestia was goddess of the hearth and the household. Apollo and Poseidon both sought to marry her; she swore on Zeus's head to remain a virgin instead. Every Greek meal began with a small offering to her at the fire.

question: The Titan king of the world was warned that one of his children would overthrow him. So each time his wife Rhea bore a baby, he swallowed it whole. Who was he?
context: Cronos's swallowed children were Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon. When Zeus was born, Rhea hid him in a Cretan cave and tricked Cronos into swallowing a stone wrapped in baby clothes instead.

question: Hidden as a baby in a Cretan cave, the youngest son of Cronos grew up secretly. He returned, freed his swallowed brothers and sisters, and led them in a ten-year war against the Titans. Who was he?
context: The war was called the Titanomachy. Zeus first forced Cronos to vomit up his swallowed children. After defeating the Titans, the brothers drew lots: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, and Hades the underworld.

question: A Titan who loved humans hid fire in a hollow fennel stalk and smuggled it down from Mount Olympus. As punishment, Zeus chained him to a mountain rock to be tortured forever. Who was he?
context: His name means 'forethought.' Each day an eagle came and ate his liver; each night it grew back. Hercules eventually killed the eagle and freed him during one of his labors. Prometheus also molded the first humans out of clay.

question: Zeus had the first woman fashioned by the gods as a punishment for humans. She was given a sealed jar and told never to open it. She opened it, and out flew every evil — only hope remained inside. What was her name?
context: Her name means 'all-gifted' — each god gave her a quality. The jar (Greek 'pithos') is often mistranslated as a box in modern retellings. Sickness, sorrow, old age, and death all escaped; hope alone stayed sealed within.

question: After the Titans lost their war against Zeus, one of them was punished by being forced to hold the entire sky on his shoulders forever. Who was he?
context: Atlas stood at the western edge of the world. Hercules once tricked him into briefly taking the sky back so Hercules could deliver the golden apples of the Hesperides. The Atlas Mountains in north Africa and the Atlantic Ocean both take their names from him.

question: Jealous Hera sent two huge serpents into the cradle of an eight-month-old baby to kill him in his sleep. The baby grabbed one snake in each tiny fist and strangled them both. What was the baby's name?
context: Hercules (Heracles in Greek) was the son of Zeus by a mortal woman, Alcmene. Hera hated him for being Zeus's child by another woman. The serpent attack was her first attempt to kill him; she would send madness on him as an adult that drove him to perform the twelve labors.

question: An Athenian prince volunteered to sail to Crete as one of fourteen Athenian young people sent every nine years to be eaten by the monstrous Minotaur. He vowed to kill the beast instead. What was his name?
context: Theseus was the son of King Aegeus of Athens. King Minos of Crete demanded the tribute as punishment for the murder of his own son. The Minotaur was half-man, half-bull, kept in a labyrinth designed by the craftsman Daedalus.

question: The hero sent to bring back Medusa's head was given a polished bronze shield by Athena to look at her reflection — since looking at her directly turned men to stone. Who was the hero?
context: Hades lent Perseus his helm of invisibility for the journey. Hermes gave him winged sandals; Athena gave him the mirror shield. Perseus used the head later to turn the sea monster Cetus to stone and save Princess Andromeda.

question: A young prince stripped of his throne sailed in a magical ship to the far end of the world to fetch the Golden Fleece. He and his fifty hand-picked heroes were called the Argonauts. What was his name?
context: The ship was the Argo, built by the craftsman Argus with a magical talking timber from Dodona at its prow. Jason's uncle Pelias set the impossible quest hoping he would die on it. The fleece came from a flying golden ram in the kingdom of Colchis.

question: A clever craftsman and his son were imprisoned in a tower on Crete. The craftsman built two pairs of wings out of feathers and beeswax so they could escape by air. What was the craftsman's name?
context: Daedalus had earlier designed the Minotaur's labyrinth for King Minos. He warned his son Icarus to fly the middle path — not too high (sun melts wax) nor too low (sea soaks feathers). Icarus flew too close to the sun and fell into the sea named after him.

question: When the Greek hero was a baby, his sea-goddess mother Thetis dipped him into the river Styx to make him invulnerable. The water did not touch the small part she held him by. Where was his one weak spot?
context: The hero was Achilles. Thetis held him by the heel as she lowered him into the underworld river. Years later at Troy, an arrow from Paris guided by Apollo struck him in that exact heel and killed him. The phrase 'Achilles heel' for a fatal weakness comes from this story.

question: A boy escaping from prison on wings of feathers and beeswax was warned by his father not to fly too close to the sun. He grew giddy with flight, soared higher, and the wax melted. What was the boy's name?
context: His father Daedalus was the craftsman who had built the wings. Icarus fell into the sea now called the Icarian Sea, near the island of Icaria off the coast of Greece. Daedalus reached Sicily alone.

question: The hero who served twelve labors for King Eurystheus wore the skin of his first kill as a cloak. The pelt could not be pierced by any weapon. What beast had he killed?
context: The hero was Hercules. Since no weapon could pierce the lion's hide, Hercules strangled it with his bare hands. He skinned it using one of its own claws (Athena had suggested it). This was the first of his twelve labors.

question: Deep inside a vast Cretan maze designed by Daedalus lived a monster with the body of a man and the head of a bull. King Minos fed Athenian youths to it every nine years. What was the monster called?
context: The Minotaur's name means 'bull of Minos.' It was the offspring of Minos's wife Pasiphae and a magnificent white bull sent by Poseidon. Theseus eventually killed it and escaped the labyrinth using a thread given to him by Princess Ariadne.

question: Three sisters lived at the end of the world with bronze claws and snakes for hair. One look at any of their faces turned a man to stone. The mortal sister was killed by Perseus. What was her name?
context: The sisters were the three Gorgons. Medusa was the only mortal one. Once a beautiful priestess of Athena, she was turned into a monster by the goddess. From her severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus.

question: When Perseus cut off Medusa's head, a magical winged creature leapt from her neck. The hero Bellerophon would later ride it to defeat the fire-breathing Chimera. What was the creature?
context: The winged horse was named Pegasus. After Bellerophon tried to ride him up to Mount Olympus to live among the gods, Zeus sent a gadfly to sting the horse — Pegasus threw Bellerophon and went up alone. Zeus placed him among the stars as a constellation.

question: The treasure Jason and the Argonauts sailed across the sea to find was the magical hide of a flying ram with wool of pure gold. In what kingdom was it kept, guarded by a never-sleeping dragon?
context: Colchis lay at the eastern end of the Black Sea. King Aeetes hid the fleece in a sacred grove of Ares. His daughter, the sorceress Medea, fell in love with Jason and used her magic to drug the dragon so Jason could steal the fleece.

question: Atop a high mountain in northern Greece, the chief gods feasted on nectar and ambrosia and held council. Lightning and clouds always hid their home from mortal eyes. What was the mountain called?
context: Mount Olympus is a real peak in northern Greece, about 9,500 feet high. The Twelve Olympians who lived there were Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, and Dionysus (sometimes Hestia in place of Dionysus).

question: Two Olympians fought for the right to be patron god of a famous Greek city. Poseidon struck the rock and a salt spring gushed out; Athena planted an olive tree. The city chose the olive. What city did she win?
context: The olive tree gave the city food, oil for lamps, and a wreath for victors. The contest is depicted on the western pediment of the Parthenon. Athens is named for Athena.

question: On the slopes of Mount Parnassus stood a temple where a priestess sat above a crack in the earth and breathed strange vapors. She gave answers from Apollo to anyone who came to ask. What was the temple's town called?
context: The priestess was called the Pythia. Apollo killed the giant serpent Python at Delphi and claimed the oracle. A stone called the Omphalos at Delphi was said to mark the navel of the world — Zeus had dropped it from above.

question: The Olympian goddess of wisdom carried a shield called the Aegis with Medusa's head set into it. Her sacred bird, often shown perched on her shoulder, was famous for its wide eyes. What bird?
context: The goddess was Athena. The Greek owl species (Athene noctua) is named after her. Owls were such common omens at Athens that the saying 'owls to Athens' meant doing something pointlessly redundant. An owl appeared on Athenian silver coins.

question: The king of the Greek gods kept a great bird as his sacred symbol. The same bird tortured Prometheus on his rock by eating his liver each day. What bird was Zeus's sacred animal?
context: Zeus sometimes took the form of an eagle himself. He sent the eagle to carry off the beautiful Trojan boy Ganymede to be cupbearer of the gods on Mount Olympus. The Romans adopted Zeus's eagle as the standard of their legions.

question: The Olympian goddess of love had a son who flew around shooting arrows at gods and mortals to make them fall in love. The Romans called him Cupid. What was his Greek name?
context: Aphrodite was Eros's mother. His golden-tipped arrows made the target love whoever they next saw; his lead-tipped arrows caused the opposite. Apollo once mocked his bow and Eros shot him with a gold arrow, making him fall hopelessly for the nymph Daphne.

question: After killing his own wife and children in a madness sent by Hera, the strongest hero of Greece was sent to King Eurystheus to atone with a long series of impossible tasks. How many labors did he have to complete?
context: The hero was Hercules. His twelve labors included slaying the Nemean Lion and the Hydra, capturing the Erymanthian Boar and the Cretan Bull, cleaning the Augean stables in a single day, fetching Cerberus from Hades, and stealing the golden apples of the Hesperides.

question: Zeus married the most beautiful goddess to the ugliest Olympian. She loved the war god Ares instead. Her smith husband once trapped them with an invisible bronze net during one of their meetings. Who was the goddess?
context: The smith husband was Hephaestus. He invited all the gods to look at the trapped lovers, then refused to release them until Poseidon promised Ares would pay Hephaestus a fine. The story is told in Book 8 of Homer's Odyssey.

question: Hades fell in love with a beautiful goddess picking flowers in a meadow. He burst up through the ground in his black chariot and dragged her down to be queen of the underworld. What was her name?
context: Persephone was the daughter of the harvest goddess Demeter. While trapped in the underworld she ate six pomegranate seeds, so she must return there each year — and her mother's grief makes the earth go cold each winter.

question: The gates of the underworld in Greek myth were guarded by a monstrous dog. Three heads barked at once and a tail of writhing snakes hissed behind. What was the dog's name?
context: Cerberus was the offspring of the monsters Typhon and Echidna. Hercules dragged him up alive to King Eurystheus as the twelfth labor. The musician Orpheus also passed Cerberus by lulling him to sleep with the lyre.

question: A mountain nymph was cursed by Hera to repeat only the last words anyone spoke. She fell hopelessly in love with a vain young man and faded away to nothing but a voice. What was the nymph's name?
context: The young man was Narcissus, who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and could not leave it. He died there and became a flower. Echo's voice still answers from rocky hillsides; that is the natural meaning of the word 'echo' today.

question: A vain young man scorned everyone who loved him, including the nymph Echo. The goddess Nemesis punished him by making him fall in love with a reflection in a pool — his own face. What was his name?
context: Narcissus stared at his reflection until he died there. A white-and-yellow flower (the narcissus, or daffodil) grew where his body had been. The word 'narcissist' for someone obsessed with their own self-image comes from this story.

question: A trickster king cheated death twice and was punished for eternity in the underworld. He must push a heavy boulder up a hill — and just before the top, it rolls back down. What was his name?
context: Sisyphus first chained up Death itself (Thanatos) to stop anyone from dying. Released, he tricked his way out of Hades a second time by telling his wife not to bury him properly. Zeus assigned the rolling boulder so his cleverness could never help him.

question: A wicked king was punished in the underworld by being placed in a pool of water beneath a fruit tree. The water shrank away whenever he bent to drink; the fruit pulled away whenever he reached. What was his name?
context: Tantalus had served his own son Pelops to the gods in a stew to test their wisdom. They saw through it at once and resurrected the boy. The English word 'tantalize' for offering something out of reach comes from his punishment.

question: At the western edge of the world, golden apples grew in a garden guarded by the Titan Atlas's daughters and a hundred-headed dragon. The fruit gave eternal youth. As his eleventh labor, who fetched some?
context: The daughters were called the Hesperides. The dragon was named Ladon. Hercules tricked Atlas into briefly taking the sky back while Hercules fetched the apples — then tricked Atlas into picking up the sky again. Hera placed the dragon in the sky as the constellation Draco.

question: Zeus turned one of his mortal loves into a snow-white heifer to hide her from his jealous wife. The wife sent a stinging gadfly to chase the cow all over the earth. What was the wife's name?
context: The mortal woman was Io, a priestess of Hera at Argos. The gadfly drove her swimming across the strait that still bears her name — the Bosporus, meaning 'cow ford.' She finally found rest in Egypt, where Zeus restored her to human form.

question: A goat-legged god of Greek shepherds played pipes made from river reeds. His shout in lonely forests could panic an entire army into terror. What was his name?
context: Pan loved a nymph named Syrinx who turned into the reeds at the riverbank to escape him; he cut and bound them into the first set of pan-pipes. The English word 'panic' for sudden terror comes from his name and his frightening shout in wild places.

question: Hercules's second labor was a swamp serpent with nine heads. Each time he cut off one head, two more grew back. With his nephew Iolaus's help, how did he stop the heads from regrowing?
context: The beast was the Lernean Hydra. Iolaus held a torch ready and seared each neck the instant Hercules cut. The central immortal head was buried under a great stone. Hercules dipped his arrows in the Hydra's poisonous blood — those arrows would kill the centaur Nessus and, later, kill Hercules himself.

question: A Phrygian king was granted any wish by the god Dionysus. He asked that everything he touched turn to gold. He grew rich at once — then his food, his wine, and his daughter all turned to gold. Who was the king?
context: Midas begged Dionysus to undo the gift. He was told to wash his hands in the river Pactolus, which afterwards ran gold-bearing for centuries. The expression 'the Midas touch' for an instinct for making money traces directly to this story.

question: The Cretan princess gave the hero a ball of string to mark his path into the maze of the Minotaur so that he could find his way back out. What was the princess's name?
context: Ariadne was the daughter of King Minos. She fell in love with Theseus, gave him the thread, and sailed away with him after he killed the Minotaur. He abandoned her on the island of Naxos, where the god Dionysus then found and married her.

question: Hera set a giant with a hundred eyes to guard the heifer Io and stop Zeus from rescuing her. Some eyes always stayed open while others slept. What was the giant's name?
context: Hermes lulled Argus to sleep with a long, dull story and his shepherd's flute, then cut off his head. Hera took the hundred eyes and set them into the tail of her sacred bird, the peacock — that is the origin of the peacock's eye-spotted tail-feathers.

question: The sun god's mortal son begged to drive his father's flaming chariot across the sky for one day. The horses bolted, scorching the earth. Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt to save the world. What was the boy's name?
context: Phaethon's father was the sun-god Helios (or Apollo in later versions). The scorched lands became the Sahara desert in some retellings, and the dark skin of the peoples of the south. His sisters wept until they were turned into poplar trees, and their tears became amber.

question: Hephaestus had three giant smith-helpers, each with a single round eye in the middle of the forehead. They forged Zeus's thunderbolts deep under a volcano. What were these one-eyed giants called?
context: The three smith-Cyclopes were named Brontes (thunder), Steropes (lightning), and Arges (bright). A different kind of Cyclops, the wild shepherd Polyphemus, would later be blinded by Odysseus in the Odyssey. Apollo killed the smith-Cyclopes in revenge for the death of his son Asclepius.

question: A Trojan prince was asked to judge which of three goddesses was the most beautiful. Each tried to bribe him. The winning goddess promised him the most beautiful mortal woman alive — and the ten-year Trojan War followed. What was the prince's name?
context: The three goddesses were Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite. Aphrodite won by promising Paris the love of Helen of Sparta — already married to King Menelaus. Paris carried her off to Troy, and Menelaus's brother Agamemnon led the Greek fleet to bring her back.

question: The most beautiful mortal woman in the world was the wife of King Menelaus of Sparta. When the Trojan prince Paris carried her off, a thousand Greek ships sailed to bring her back. What was her name?
context: Helen was the daughter of Zeus by Leda, who Zeus had visited in the form of a swan. Her face was said to be the one 'that launched a thousand ships.' The Trojan War lasted ten years, ending with the wooden horse and the burning of Troy.

question: After ten years of failed siege, the Greeks built a huge hollow wooden gift, hid soldiers inside, and pretended to sail away. The Trojans dragged it into their walls. By morning, Troy was in flames. What was the gift?
context: The clever idea was Odysseus's. The Trojan priest Laocoön and the princess Cassandra both warned that the gift was a trick, but no one listened — Cassandra had been cursed always to be right but never believed. The English saying 'beware Greeks bearing gifts' comes from this story.

question: A Trojan princess was given the gift of true prophecy by the god Apollo when he hoped to win her love. She refused him, and he punished her by adding a curse so that her true predictions would never be believed. Who was she?
context: Cassandra was a daughter of King Priam of Troy. She foretold the fall of Troy, warned against the wooden horse, and predicted her own murder at the hands of Queen Clytemnestra after the war. Each prediction came true; no one ever believed her.

question: The greatest warrior of Troy was the eldest son of King Priam. He fought Achilles in single combat outside the walls of Troy and was killed in front of his own family watching from the towers. Who was he?
context: Hector's wife was Andromache and his small son was Astyanax. Achilles dragged Hector's body three times around the walls of Troy behind his chariot. King Priam later went alone into the Greek camp to beg for his son's body back — one of the most moving scenes in Homer's Iliad.

question: The Greek king of Ithaca took ten years to sail home from the Trojan War, blown off course by storms and angry gods. His wife Penelope waited and his son Telemachus grew up missing him. What was the king's name?
context: Odysseus blinded the Cyclops Polyphemus, escaped the Sirens, lost his men to Scylla and Charybdis, spent seven years with the nymph Calypso, and finally returned home disguised as a beggar. His ten years home, plus the ten years of the war, became the original meaning of the word 'odyssey.'

question: Eris, the goddess of discord, was not invited to a wedding feast on Olympus. In revenge she tossed a single golden apple into the hall, marked 'for the fairest.' Three goddesses — Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite — each claimed it. Zeus refused to judge and sent them to a Trojan shepherd-prince. What did Aphrodite promise to win?
answer: Helen of Sparta as his wife
choices: Helen of Sparta as his wife
Kingship over Asia and the East
Wisdom above all other mortal men
Strength to defeat any warrior alive
context: The shepherd was Paris, secretly a prince of Troy raised in the hills. Hera offered him rule of Asia; Athena offered him wisdom and victory in battle; Aphrodite won with Helen — the wife of King Menelaus of Sparta. Paris carried her off, and the ten-year Trojan War followed.

question: After ten years of failed siege at Troy, the Greek army built a huge hollow wooden horse, hid soldiers inside, and pretended to sail away as if defeated. The Trojans, thinking it an offering to Athena, dragged the horse inside their walls and celebrated all night. Whose clever idea was the trick?
choices: Agamemnon, the high king of Mycenae
Diomedes, son of King Tydeus of Argos
context: At midnight Odysseus and his men slipped out of the horse, opened the gates, and let in the rest of the Greek army that had quietly returned. Troy was sacked and burned by morning. The Trojan priest Laocoön had shouted to beware Greeks bearing gifts — and was strangled by sea serpents sent by Athena before he could be heeded.

question: A young princess of Troy was given the gift of true prophecy by Apollo when he hoped to win her love. When she still refused him, he could not take the gift back — so he added a second curse on top: every true thing she foretold would be disbelieved. She warned against the wooden horse. She warned of her own murder. What was her name?
context: Cassandra was a daughter of King Priam. After Troy fell, she was taken back to Greece as a prize by King Agamemnon. She predicted that his wife Clytemnestra would murder them both the night they arrived — and she was right, again. Her name now means 'a true prophet whose warnings are ignored.'

question: When Achilles refused to fight at Troy because of an insult from King Agamemnon, his dearest friend put on Achilles's own armor and led his men into battle to push the Trojans back from the Greek ships. The hero Hector killed him before the gates of Troy. What was the friend's name?
context: Patroclus's death broke Achilles's wrath. Achilles returned to the battle in new armor forged by Hephaestus himself, killed Hector, dragged his body three times around the walls of Troy behind his chariot, and finally died from an arrow through the heel shot by Paris with Apollo's guidance.

question: The greatest warrior of Troy went out to fight Achilles in single combat after Achilles's friend Patroclus had been killed. His wife begged him at the city gate not to go, holding their small son. The baby cried at the gleam on his father's helmet. What was the warrior's name?
context: His wife was Andromache; their son was Astyanax. Hector took off the frightening helmet to lift the boy. Then he went out to die. After the city fell, Astyanax was thrown from the walls by the victorious Greeks and Andromache was taken as a slave by Achilles's son Neoptolemus.

question: After killing Hector before the walls of Troy, the Greek hero stripped off his armor, tied the body by the heels to his chariot, and rode three times around the city in full view of Hector's family on the walls. Old King Priam himself eventually came alone to the Greek camp to beg for the body back. Who was the Greek hero?
context: Priam came at night, guided by Hermes, and kissed the hands of the man who had killed his son. Achilles wept with him. He allowed the Trojans twelve days of truce to bury Hector with full honors. The scene is the closing book of Homer's Iliad.

question: After killing Hector, the greatest Greek warrior fought on at Troy until the day a single arrow struck him in the only part of his body where his mother had not dipped him in the river Styx. Paris, his weakest enemy, fired the arrow; Apollo guided it. Where did the arrow strike?
context: The hero was Achilles. His sea-goddess mother Thetis had dipped him as a baby in the underworld river Styx, but the water did not touch the heel she held him by. The phrase 'Achilles heel' for any one fatal weakness in an otherwise strong person comes directly from this story.

question: Before there was a Trojan War, the most beautiful mortal woman in the world had so many suitors that her father made them all swear an oath together — that whichever man she chose, the others would defend her marriage by force if anyone ever tried to steal her. When Paris carried her off, the oath called a thousand Greek ships. Whose oath was it?
context: Tyndareus was Helen's mortal father (Zeus was her real father, by Leda in the form of a swan). She chose Menelaus, brother of King Agamemnon of Mycenae. When Paris of Troy seduced her away, every oath-bound suitor across Greece — Odysseus, Diomedes, Ajax, and a hundred more — had to sail to Troy.

question: The wedding of King Peleus and the sea-nymph Thetis (the future parents of Achilles) was attended by every god on Olympus — except one, who had been left off the guest list on purpose. In revenge she rolled a single golden apple into the feast inscribed 'for the fairest.' Who was the goddess?
context: Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite each claimed the apple. Zeus made the Trojan prince Paris judge between them, and so the whole long Trojan War spiralled from that single apple. The phrase 'apple of discord' for any small thing that starts a big fight comes from this story.

question: The Greek fleet sailed to Troy under the high king Agamemnon. But the wind died at Aulis. The priest Calchas said the goddess Artemis was angry; only one sacrifice would free the wind. Who did Agamemnon order brought to the altar?
context: Some versions say Artemis snatched Iphigenia from the altar at the last moment, replacing her with a deer; others say Agamemnon truly killed her. The wind blew. Years later, when Agamemnon came home from the war, his wife Clytemnestra remembered what he had done — and killed him on his return.

question: Sailing home from Troy, the Greek hero Odysseus and his men were trapped in the cave of a one-eyed giant called Polyphemus. The giant was eating two of them every meal. Odysseus blinded him with a burning olivewood stake while he slept, and they escaped clinging to the wool of his sheep. When the giant roared for help, Odysseus had told him a fake name. What was it?
context: When the other Cyclopes came running and shouted in through the cave-mouth 'Who hurts you, Polyphemus?', he could only shout back 'Nobody is hurting me!' — and they laughed and went back to bed. Polyphemus was the son of Poseidon, who pursued Odysseus with storms all the way home.

question: On his long voyage home, Odysseus had to sail past an island where bird-women sang so sweetly that any sailor who heard them would steer his ship onto the rocks. The witch Circe had warned him. He stuffed his sailors' ears with beeswax. What did he have his men do with him?
choices: Lock him in the ship's hold
Steer the ship themselves while he slept
Cover his eyes with a heavy cloth
context: Odysseus alone among Greek sailors heard the Sirens' song and lived. He left his ears open because he wanted to hear it. He begged his men to release him; they tied him tighter, and rowed harder. The Sirens, it was said, were doomed to die if any mortal heard them and escaped — they hurled themselves into the sea.

question: On the island of Aiaia, a beautiful witch invited the lost crew of Odysseus to a feast. She drugged their wine and touched them with her wand. They grew bristles, dropped to all fours, and ran into the pen squealing. What had she turned them into?
context: The witch was Circe, daughter of the sun-god Helios. Odysseus drank her potion safely because Hermes had given him a magical herb called moly. When she could not enchant him, he forced her to turn the men back. He lived as her lover for a year before sailing on toward home.

question: Shipwrecked alone on a green island after losing his last crew, the hero Odysseus was kept seven years by a beautiful goddess who offered him immortality if he would stay forever. He sat each evening on the shore weeping for home. Zeus finally sent Hermes to order her to let him go. What was the goddess's name?
context: Her name means 'she who hides.' Her island Ogygia was at the navel of the sea. She helped Odysseus build a raft when she finally released him; the sea-god Poseidon promptly wrecked it. Odysseus reached the next island clinging to a single beam.

question: While her husband Odysseus was missing for twenty years, his wife was pressed by a crowd of suitors who feasted in her hall and demanded she remarry. She told them she would choose a new husband once she finished weaving the shroud for her father-in-law Laertes. Each day she wove. Each night she did what?
answer: Unwove what she had woven by day
choices: Unwove what she had woven by day
Began a new garment in secret
Burned the loom in fits of grief
Sent the cloth to her son Telemachus
context: The wife was Penelope. Her trick held off the suitors for three years before a maid betrayed her. When Odysseus came home in disguise as a beggar, Penelope set the final test that proved his identity: only the true Odysseus could string his old great bow.

question: Returning home to Ithaca after twenty years, Odysseus disguised himself as a beggar and entered his own hall, where over a hundred suitors courted his wife. Penelope announced a contest: she would marry whichever man could string Odysseus's old bow and shoot an arrow through twelve lined-up axes. What happened when the suitors tried?
answer: None could even bend the bow to string it
choices: None could even bend the bow to string it
Each shot was deflected by the gods
Only Telemachus succeeded in stringing it
The bow snapped in the strongest suitor's grip
context: The disguised beggar then asked his turn. He strung the great bow with one easy motion, shot through all twelve axe-heads — and turned the next arrow on the suitors. With his son Telemachus, the swineherd Eumaeus, and the cowherd Philoetius, he killed every suitor in the hall.

question: Odysseus had to sail his ship through a narrow strait between two monsters. On one side was a six-headed sea-monster that snatched sailors off ship-decks; on the other a huge whirlpool that swallowed entire boats. He was told he must choose one. Circe advised him to keep close to the monster, not the whirlpool. What was the monster's name?
context: Scylla was the six-headed monster; Charybdis was the whirlpool. Odysseus lost six men to Scylla's mouths but saved his ship; passing close to Charybdis would have sunk all hands. The phrase 'between Scylla and Charybdis' still means choosing between two dangers when no safe path exists.

question: When the disguised beggar Odysseus came home to Ithaca, the only one to recognize him at first was his old nurse, washing his feet for the night. She felt a long scar on his thigh and almost cried out — but he gripped her by the throat and warned her to be silent. Where had he gotten that scar long ago?
answer: From a wild boar's tusk on Mount Parnassus
choices: From a wild boar's tusk on Mount Parnassus
From the spear of a Trojan named Pandarus
From his fall as a child off the palace wall
From the wing of the bird Stymphalian on a hunt
context: The nurse was Eurycleia. Odysseus had been gored on a boar hunt as a young man visiting his grandfather Autolycus. The recognition scene in Odyssey 19 is one of the most famous moments in ancient literature; the German philosopher Erich Auerbach used it to open his book 'Mimesis' on the Western literary tradition.

question: After twenty years away, Odysseus reached home disguised as a beggar so even his wife could not recognize him. One creature in the courtyard knew him at once — an old, flea-bitten animal lying on a dung heap that lifted its head, wagged what was left of its tail, and died of joy. What was the creature?
context: Argos had been a puppy when Odysseus left for Troy. He was now twenty years old and forgotten on a dung pile outside the gate. The scene is in Odyssey 17. Odysseus could not even pat him — he had to keep his disguise — and turned away with a tear before entering the hall.

question: Early on his way home from Troy, Odysseus landed on an island where the people lived by eating the fruit of a strange plant. Anyone who tasted it forgot home and family entirely, and wanted only to lie under the trees eating more. He had to drag his weeping crew back to the ships in chains. What was the plant?
context: The episode is in Odyssey 9. The phrase 'lotus eaters' for people lost in soft pleasures while neglecting duties at home comes directly from this story. Tennyson wrote a famous Victorian poem 'The Lotos-Eaters' retelling it.

question: For his first labor under King Eurystheus, the strongest hero of Greece was sent to bring back the skin of a lion whose hide could not be pierced by arrow or sword. He tracked the beast to its two-mouthed cave, blocked one entrance with boulders, and confronted it inside. Since weapons were useless, how did he kill it?
answer: He strangled it with his bare hands
choices: He strangled it with his bare hands
He shot it with the bow of Apollo
He drowned it in the River Styx
He starved it shut in its own cave
context: The hero was Hercules; the beast was the Nemean Lion. Afterwards he wore its pelt as armor — nothing could pierce it. Skinning it was almost impossible until Athena suggested using one of the lion's own claws. The constellation Leo honors the lion.

question: Volunteering as one of fourteen Athenian young people to be eaten by the Minotaur on Crete, the prince Theseus arrived in chains. King Minos's own daughter fell in love with him and gave him something at the labyrinth entrance that let him kill the beast AND find his way back out again. What did she give him?
answer: A ball of thread to mark his path back
choices: A ball of thread to mark his path back
An enchanted bronze sword that glowed in the dark
A magic helmet that turned him invisible
A pair of winged sandals from Hermes
context: The princess was Ariadne. Theseus tied the thread at the entrance and unwound it as he went. After killing the Minotaur with his bare hands, he followed the thread back to her. She sailed away with him toward Athens, but he abandoned her on the island of Naxos — where the god Dionysus then found and married her.

question: Sent on what should have been an impossible errand by a king who wanted him dead, the hero Perseus tracked the three snake-haired Gorgon sisters to a cave at the world's western end. Looking at any of their faces turned a man to stone. Athena gave him a polished bronze shield. How did he avoid Medusa's gaze?
answer: He watched her in the shield's reflection
choices: He watched her in the shield's reflection
He blindfolded himself with Athena's veil
He fought her with eyes squeezed shut
He killed her sisters first while she slept
context: Perseus also carried winged sandals from Hermes, a helm of invisibility from Hades, and a curved sword from Hephaestus. From Medusa's severed neck leapt the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor. He used her preserved head as a weapon to turn his enemies to stone.

question: Flying home from killing Medusa, Perseus saw a princess chained to a rock by the sea as a sacrifice to a sea-monster. Her mother had boasted of being more beautiful than the sea-nymphs. He killed the monster and married the princess on the spot. What was her name?
context: Andromeda's mother was Cassiopeia, queen of Ethiopia. Both mother (the boasting one) and daughter (the rescued one) are now constellations in the night sky, along with Cepheus the father, Perseus, and the sea-monster Cetus. The story of a sea-monster, a chained princess, and a hero on a flying steed shaped the dragon-rescuing-knight tales of medieval Europe.

question: A young prince stripped of his throne was sent on a quest his uncle expected him to die on — to sail to the kingdom of Colchis at the eastern edge of the world and bring back the magical hide of a flying golden ram, guarded by a never-sleeping dragon. He built a ship called the Argo. What was the prince's name?
context: Jason gathered fifty of the greatest heroes of Greece — the Argonauts — including Hercules, Theseus, Orpheus, Atalanta, Castor and Pollux. The princess of Colchis, the sorceress Medea, fell in love with Jason and used her magic to drug the dragon so he could steal the fleece. She fled with him and was later betrayed by him.

question: The craftsman who had built the labyrinth for King Minos was later imprisoned with his son in a high tower on Crete. He built two pairs of wings out of feathers and beeswax so the two could escape by air. He warned his son to fly the middle path — not too low (sea soaks feathers) and not too high. What happened to the son?
answer: He flew too close to the sun and fell into the sea
choices: He flew too close to the sun and fell into the sea
He landed safely with his father in Sicily
Apollo struck him down with a golden arrow
Poseidon sent a great wave to capture him
context: The craftsman was Daedalus and the son was Icarus. The wax of Icarus's wings melted in the heat. He drowned in the sea now named the Icarian Sea, off an island called Icaria. Daedalus reached Sicily alone, where he later built King Cocalus a temple to Apollo.

question: A great huntress would marry only a man who could outrun her in a foot race. She killed the losers. A clever suitor named Hippomenes prayed to Aphrodite and was given three golden apples. Each time the huntress drew ahead, he threw one in her path and she stopped to pick it up. Who was the huntress?
context: Atalanta had been left on a mountainside as a baby by a father who wanted a son. A bear nursed her and hunters raised her. She was the only woman to sail on the Argo and the first to strike the Calydonian Boar in the great hunt. She married Hippomenes after he won — but the two later angered Aphrodite and she turned them both into lions.

question: A cunning king of Corinth twice cheated Death itself. The first time he caught Death in chains so no one in the world could die. The second time he tricked his way out of Hades by ordering his wife not to bury him properly. Zeus finally sentenced him for eternity to roll something heavy up a hill. What?
answer: A boulder that always rolls back down
choices: A boulder that always rolls back down
A vat of wine he could never empty
A chariot wheel that never stops turning
A pillar of marble taller than he could lift
context: The king was Sisyphus. The boulder always rolled back just before the summit. The French writer Albert Camus used the image as a picture of the absurd in his essay 'The Myth of Sisyphus' (1942). The English adjective 'Sisyphean' for any endless, hopeless task comes from his name.

question: A king tried to test the gods at a feast by serving them a stew made from his own son Pelops. The gods saw through the trick at once, resurrected the boy, and threw the king down to the underworld. They placed him in a pool of water beneath a fruit tree — yet he could never drink and never eat. Who was the king?
context: The water shrank away whenever Tantalus bent to drink; the fruit pulled back whenever he reached. The English word 'tantalize' for showing someone something desirable and then yanking it out of reach comes directly from his punishment. His son Pelops grew up to give his name to the Peloponnese, the southern part of Greece.

question: When the nymph Eurydice died of a snake bite on her wedding day, her grieving husband took only his lyre and descended into the underworld. His music made Hades and Persephone weep and they granted him an impossible gift — but on one condition as he led Eurydice back. What was the condition?
answer: Do not look back at her until both are out
choices: Do not look back at her until both are out
Do not speak her name on the journey home
Do not let her touch the surface light first
Do not bury his lyre when he reached the world above
context: The husband was Orpheus. Just before reaching the cave-mouth at the upper world, doubt seized him and he turned to make sure she was still there — and she vanished forever. He wandered Thrace afterwards refusing to play music for anyone. Frenzied followers of Dionysus eventually tore him apart, and his severed head floated singing down a river to Lesbos.

question: A Cypriot sculptor who scorned all real women carved an ivory statue of his ideal woman and fell in love with the statue. He kissed it and dressed it as if it were alive. He prayed to Aphrodite at her festival. When he came home and kissed the statue's mouth one more time, what happened?
answer: Her ivory warmed and softened into living flesh
choices: Her ivory warmed and softened into living flesh
She spoke aloud and named herself Galatea
Aphrodite herself appeared as the statue
His own sculpting tools came to life and danced
context: The sculptor was Pygmalion. He married the living woman and they named their daughter Paphos, who gave her name to a town on Cyprus sacred to Aphrodite. George Bernard Shaw wrote a play 'Pygmalion' (1913) about a phonetics professor remaking a flower girl, which became the musical 'My Fair Lady.'

question: For his fifth labor, Hercules was ordered to clean the cattle stables of King Augeas in a single day. The stables held thousands of cattle and had not been mucked out in thirty years. He could not possibly shovel them in one day. What did he do instead?
answer: Diverted two rivers to wash the stables clean
choices: Diverted two rivers to wash the stables clean
Set the entire stable on fire at sunrise
Called every vulture from the hills to feed
Built tall walls of dung and walked away
context: The rivers were the Alpheios and the Peneios. King Augeas had promised Hercules a tenth of his cattle but refused to pay once the labor was done — claiming Hercules had only completed it for Eurystheus, not for hire. Hercules later returned with an army and killed him.

question: While Persephone was picking flowers in a meadow with friends, the ground burst open beneath her and Hades carried her down in his chariot to be queen of the underworld. Her mother Demeter froze the earth in grief. Zeus ordered her returned — but Hades had already tricked her into eating something small. What?
choices: A single black fig from the underworld
A spoonful of broth at his table
A dark grape from his own vine
context: Anyone who eats food in the underworld must remain. The deal was struck — Persephone would spend one third of the year (in some tellings half) with Hades and the rest with her mother. Demeter's mourning during the underworld months became winter; her joy at her daughter's return became spring.

question: Hades, lord of the underworld, fell in love with a young goddess picking flowers in a meadow in Sicily one spring. He burst up through the ground in his black chariot pulled by four black horses and carried her down. Who was the goddess?
context: Persephone was the daughter of Demeter, goddess of grain and the harvest. Demeter searched every land for her with two torches, refusing to let any seed sprout until Persephone was returned. The story explains the change of the seasons: winter is Demeter's grief while Persephone is in the underworld.

question: A mountain nymph who could speak only by repeating the last words of others fell in love with a beautiful young man named Narcissus. He laughed at her and ran away. She faded until only her voice remained. The goddess Nemesis then took revenge on him. How?
answer: Made him fall in love with his own reflection
choices: Made him fall in love with his own reflection
Turned him into a yellow narcissus flower at once
Sent ravens to peck out his beautiful eyes
Tied him to a tree until he wasted away
context: The nymph was Echo. Narcissus stared at his reflection in a still pool until he died of hunger and thirst; a white-and-yellow flower (the narcissus) grew where his body had been. The words 'echo' and 'narcissist' both come from this single story.

question: When her daughter was kidnapped to the underworld, the goddess of grain and the harvest searched the whole earth carrying two torches. She refused to let any seed sprout or any plant grow until her daughter was returned. The world began to starve. Who was the goddess?
context: Demeter eventually went to dwell in disguise as a nursemaid in the household of King Celeus at Eleusis. The secret rites that grew up around her there — the Eleusinian Mysteries — were the most famous mystery religion of the ancient Greek world, lasting nearly 2,000 years before the Christian emperor Theodosius shut them down.

question: For stealing fire from Mount Olympus and giving it to mortals, the Titan Prometheus was chained by Zeus to a rock in the Caucasus Mountains. Each day a giant bird came down and tore something out of him, which then grew back overnight. What did the bird eat?
context: The bird was a great eagle, sacred to Zeus. The Greeks thought of the liver (not the heart) as the seat of feeling and life-force — making the choice especially cruel. Hercules eventually shot the eagle and freed Prometheus during his journey to fetch the apples of the Hesperides.

question: Zeus had the first mortal woman fashioned by the gods and given as a punishment to humans after Prometheus stole fire. She was named Pandora — 'all-gifted.' Each god gave her a quality. Hermes added a curious mind and a lying tongue. She was given a sealed jar and told never to open it. She opened it. What was left inside when she slammed the lid shut?
context: Every other evil — sickness, sorrow, old age, war, hatred, hard labor, death — flew out of the jar and into the world before she could close it. The jar (Greek pithos) is mistranslated as a box in many retellings; the scholar Erasmus made the mistranslation in the 16th century and it has stuck. Hope alone remained.

question: After Zeus's gods defeated the Titans, one Titan was punished by being made to hold the entire sky on his shoulders forever, at the western edge of the world. Hercules tricked him into briefly taking the sky back during the labor of the golden apples. Who was the Titan?
context: The Atlas Mountains in north Africa and the Atlantic Ocean both take their names from him. A book of maps came to be called an 'atlas' after a 16th-century edition published by Mercator showed him on the cover holding up the world. Atlas's daughters included the Pleiades, now a famous star cluster.

question: The mortal son of the sun-god Helios begged to drive his father's flaming chariot across the sky for one day to prove his parentage. The horses sensed a weak driver and bolted from the path, scorching the earth. Zeus had to stop the world from burning. How?
answer: He struck the boy from the chariot with a thunderbolt
choices: He struck the boy from the chariot with a thunderbolt
He sent Hermes to grab the reins of the horses
He poured the river Eridanus over the burning earth
He made the chariot turn itself to ice in mid-flight
context: The boy was Phaethon. His sisters wept so long that they were turned into poplar trees lining the river Eridanus, and their tears became amber drops in its mud. The scorched lands in the south were said to explain the deserts of north Africa and the darker skin of the peoples who lived there.

question: A young hero from Corinth was sent to kill the Chimera — a fire-breathing monster with the head of a lion, the body of a goat, and the tail of a serpent. He could not approach her on foot. With the goddess Athena's help he tamed the winged horse Pegasus by bridling him at a spring. What was the hero's name?
context: Bellerophon killed the Chimera by jamming a lead-tipped spear down her throat from above; her own fiery breath melted the lead and choked her. Later Bellerophon tried to ride Pegasus up to Mount Olympus to live among the gods. Zeus sent a gadfly to sting the horse; Pegasus threw Bellerophon, who fell to earth crippled.

question: The wooden horse left outside the gates of Troy was found beside a single Greek soldier left chained to it, weeping that his own army had abandoned him as a sacrifice to the gods for safe winds home. He begged Troy for mercy and convinced the Trojans the horse was a gift. What was his name?
context: Sinon was Odysseus's cousin and part of the trick from the beginning. His convincing tale of betrayal got the Trojans to drag the horse inside their walls. The Trojan priest Laocoön shouted 'Beware Greeks bearing gifts!' and was promptly strangled by sea serpents sent by Athena — Cassandra also warned, but no one believed her either.

question: When the great wooden horse appeared outside Troy after the Greek ships sailed away, one Trojan priest threw his spear into the horse's flank and shouted his famous warning to his fellow Trojans. Almost at once two huge sea serpents rose from the waves and crushed him and his two sons to death in their coils. What was the priest's name?
context: Laocoön's famous warning has come down as 'Beware Greeks bearing gifts.' The marble sculpture of him and his sons fighting the serpents — found in Rome in 1506 — is one of the most celebrated ancient statues in the world, now in the Vatican Museums. It powerfully influenced Michelangelo, who saw it dug up.

question: After Hector killed Patroclus in Achilles's borrowed armor, Achilles had no gear to return to battle in. His sea-goddess mother Thetis went up to Mount Olympus and begged the smith god to forge him new armor in a single night. The shield was decorated with whole scenes of the cosmos. Who forged it?
context: Homer describes the Shield of Achilles in nearly 130 lines of the Iliad (Book 18) — earth, sky, sea, the constellations, two cities (one at peace, one at war), a king's vineyard at harvest, a wedding, a murder trial, a dance. It is one of the earliest and most famous works of ekphrasis (vivid word-description of a visual work) in Western literature.

question: For one labor, Hercules was sent to drive a flock of monstrous man-eating birds away from a lake. They had bronze beaks, bronze claws, and feathers they could shoot like arrows. Hercules could not approach them through the marsh. What did Athena give him to scare them into flight?
context: The rattle (sometimes called krotala) was made by Hephaestus. Hercules climbed a hill and shook the rattle until the noise drove the birds into the air, then shot them down one by one with his bow. The birds were sacred to Ares; the survivors flew east to the island where Jason and the Argonauts later met them.

question: For his fourth labor, Hercules had to bring back a monstrous wild boar alive from the snowy slopes of Mount Erymanthus. He chased it on foot through deep snow until the beast was exhausted. He then carried it on his shoulders to the palace. When King Eurystheus saw it, what did he do?
answer: Hid in a large bronze storage jar in terror
choices: Hid in a large bronze storage jar in terror
Sent his guards to wrestle it for sport
Demanded Hercules cook it for the feast
Released it at once into his hunting park
context: Eurystheus had ordered Hercules brought to him with the live boar over his shoulder. The sight of Hercules carrying the snarling beast was too much. From then on Eurystheus ordered Hercules to show each kill from outside the city walls, and is said to have kept the bronze jar nearby. The vase-painters of Greece loved the scene.

question: Half-horse, half-human creatures lived wild in the mountains of Thessaly and were always fighting humans, especially at weddings, where they would get drunk and try to carry off the bride. The wisest of them was the centaur Chiron, who tutored many heroes. What were these creatures called?
context: Chiron tutored Asclepius, Jason, Achilles, and others. The centaur Nessus tried to carry off Hercules's wife Deianira at a river crossing and was shot through with Hercules's poisoned arrow — but his dying blood, given to her as a 'love charm,' eventually killed Hercules years later. The constellation Centaurus marks them in the southern sky.

question: Searching for his sister Europa (whom Zeus had carried off as a white bull), a Phoenician prince consulted the oracle at Delphi and was told to follow a cow until it lay down — and to found a city there. To clear the ground he killed a dragon sacred to Ares and sowed its teeth in the earth. What sprang up?
context: The prince was Cadmus. The armed warriors fought each other to the death except for five survivors, who became the first noble families of the city he founded — Thebes. Cadmus was also credited by the Greeks with bringing the alphabet from Phoenicia to Greece. He and his wife Harmonia were eventually turned into a pair of serpents.

question: On the road to Thebes, a young traveler met a winged monster with the body of a lion, the wings of an eagle, and the head of a woman. She would let no one pass who could not answer her riddle. He answered. She threw herself off the cliff in defeat. What was the monster called?
context: The traveler was Oedipus and the riddle was: 'What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening?' Answer: a human (crawling baby, walking adult, leaning on a staff in old age). His reward was the throne of Thebes and the hand of the widowed queen Jocasta — who, he would later learn to his horror, was his own mother.

question: A goat-legged nature god chased a beautiful river nymph. To escape him she begged the river to change her shape, and her sisters turned her into a bed of tall reeds at the water's edge. The god sat down by the reeds, cut some, and bound them together. What did he make?
context: The god was Pan and the nymph was Syrinx — her name still attached to the instrument 'syrinx' (the Greek word for pan-pipes). Pan's lonely shouts in wild forests were said to be enough to make any traveler flee in 'panic' — that English word comes directly from his name.

question: After Apollo mocked the small bow of Eros, the love-god shot him with a gold-tipped arrow and shot the nymph Daphne with a lead-tipped one — making Apollo love her hopelessly and Daphne hate him. He chased her through the woods. Just as he caught her, she begged her river-god father to save her. What did her father do?
answer: Turned her into a laurel tree
choices: Turned her into a laurel tree
Hid her in his river-bed forever
Lifted her up into the night sky as a star
Changed her into a swift white doe
context: Apollo embraced the tree and made the laurel his sacred plant. Crowns of laurel were given to winning athletes at the Pythian Games and to victorious Roman generals. The phrase 'resting on one's laurels' comes from this — and the Italian sculptor Bernini's Apollo and Daphne (1625) shows the moment of transformation.

question: Two brothers (one mortal, one immortal) sailed with Jason on the Argo and went on so many heroic adventures together that when the mortal one was finally killed, the immortal one refused to live without him. Zeus placed them together as a constellation. What constellation are they?
context: The brothers were Castor (mortal) and Pollux (immortal son of Zeus). Pollux begged to share his immortality so they could be together. Zeus made them spend alternate days in the underworld and on Olympus, and set them in the sky as the constellation Gemini. They were the patron gods of Roman sailors, and 'gemini' means simply 'twins' in Latin.

question: King Oeneus of Calydon forgot to sacrifice to Artemis at harvest, and the goddess sent a monstrous boar to ravage his lands. He gathered the greatest hunters in Greece — including Atalanta, the huntress raised by a bear. Atalanta drew first blood. Who finally killed the boar?
context: Meleager gave the boar's hide to Atalanta because she had drawn first blood. His uncles tried to seize it, claiming a woman should not be honored above them. Meleager killed his uncles. His mother — their sister — threw a magical log onto the fire that fate had bound to his life; as it burned, he died.

question: To reach the kingdom of the dead in Greek myth, a soul had to be ferried across an underground river by a grim old boatman. He charged a single coin for the passage. The Greeks placed a coin under each dead person's tongue to pay the fare. What was the river called?
context: The boatman was Charon. Souls of those who had not been properly buried, or who had no coin, wandered the near shore for a hundred years. Hercules and Odysseus and Aeneas all crossed alive — special cases. The coin was called an obol, and the custom of 'Charon's obol' lasted in some places until late antiquity.

question: Walking on Mount Cithaeron, a young man saw two snakes mating, struck them with his staff, and was turned into a woman for seven years. Seven years later he saw the snakes again, struck again, and was turned back into a man. The gods later made him blind but gave him true prophecy. What was his name?
context: Zeus and Hera asked Tiresias to settle their argument over whether men or women had more pleasure in love. Tiresias (having been both) said women did — by far. Hera blinded him in anger; Zeus could not undo her curse but gave him prophecy in compensation. Odysseus consulted his ghost in Odyssey 11.

question: Three winged goddesses with snakes in their hair and brass-clawed hands hunted down murderers — especially those who had killed their own family — and drove them mad with screams and torches. They were so feared that the Greeks called them by a flattering name instead, 'the Kindly Ones.' What were they called?
context: The three Furies were Alecto, Megaera, and Tisiphone. They were born from the blood of Uranus when Cronos castrated him. In Aeschylus's play 'The Eumenides' (458 BC), the goddess Athena persuaded them to stop hounding Orestes for killing his mother — and gave them a new home as 'Kindly Ones' beneath the rock of the Areopagus in Athens.

question: Three sister goddesses spun the thread of every mortal's life. One drew it from the distaff, one measured its length, and the third cut it at the moment of death. Not even Zeus himself could undo what they had done. What were they called?
context: The three sisters were Clotho the spinner, Lachesis the measurer, and Atropos ('the unbendable') who held the shears. The Romans called them the Parcae. The English word 'fate' comes from Latin 'fatum' — 'that which has been spoken' (by the Fates). Even gods kept clear of them.

question: Nine sister-goddesses on Mount Helicon inspired every poet, musician, dancer, and historian in Greece. They were daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, the Titan of memory. Every great epic poem in ancient Greece began by calling on one of them by name. What were they?
context: The nine were Calliope (epic poetry), Clio (history), Erato (love poetry), Euterpe (music), Melpomene (tragedy), Polyhymnia (sacred song), Terpsichore (dance), Thalia (comedy), and Urania (astronomy). The English words 'music' and 'museum' (literally 'shrine of the Muses') both come from their name.

question: Among the wild centaurs of Mount Pelion lived one who was wise, learned, and immortal — a tutor to many of the greatest Greek heroes. He raised Jason, taught Achilles, trained the healer Asclepius, and counseled Hercules. What was his name?
context: Chiron was accidentally wounded by one of Hercules's poisoned arrows. The pain was so terrible that, although immortal, he begged Zeus to release him into death. Zeus did, and placed him in the sky as the constellation Centaurus (or Sagittarius, by some accounts). His name gave us the English word 'surgery' through the Greek word 'kheirourgos' (handcraft).

question: After her daughter was kidnapped to the underworld, the grain-goddess wandered the earth disguised as a nursemaid. She came to the household of King Celeus at Eleusis and tried to make their baby boy immortal by holding him in the fire each night. The mother caught her at it and screamed. What did the goddess do then?
answer: Revealed herself in full divine glory
choices: Revealed herself in full divine glory
Turned the baby into a young stag instantly
Vanished without a word and left no trace
Cursed the household with a long famine
context: The goddess was Demeter. She ordered the household of Eleusis to build her a temple and there she instituted the Eleusinian Mysteries — the most famous mystery religion of the ancient Greek world. Initiates were sworn to secrecy on pain of death; the rites lasted for nearly two thousand years before the Christian emperor Theodosius shut them down.
